metadata.original_text: This time series records cost of living data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-12-21 to 2026-03-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On December 2, 2025, the Brookings Institution published a report analyzing the cost of living across 160 U.S. metro areas. The analysis revealed that one-third of the American middle class can no longer afford basic necessities, such as food, housing, and child care, due to local income ranges and price variations. <2> On November 1, 2025, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) announced the 2026 conforming loan limits, increasing the baseline limit to $832,750 for single-unit properties in most of the U.S. to account for a rise in average home prices. <3> On November 20, 2025, Ipsos released its 2025 Cost of Living Monitor, which revealed that 65% of Americans expect inflation to rise in 2026. This marks a significant 14-percentage-point increase from the previous year, reflecting heightened economic concerns driven by perceptions of price gouging and corporate greed. <4> On November 14, 2025, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced the 2026 Medicare Part A and B premiums and deductibles. The standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B will increase to $202.90, up $17.90 from the 2025 rate of $185.00, while the Part B deductible will be $283 and the Part A deductible will reach $1,736. These increases are attributed to projected price changes and rising demand for healthcare services, reflecting an overall increase in medical costs. The higher costs will disproportionately burden older adults on fixed incomes, as the premium hike will consume over a quarter of the anticipated 2.8 percent Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). <5> The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) announced the 2026 cost-of-living adjustments for retirement plans, increasing the maximum annual elective salary deferral for 401(k), 403(b), and most 457 plans from $23,500 to $24,500 to account for inflation. <6> S&P Global Mobility projected new light vehicle sales in the U.S. for October 2025 would reach 1.29 million units, translating to a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of 15.6 million units. This forecast indicates a slight increase from the previous year but represents a moderation from the strong sales of the third quarter. The third quarter's results were significantly boosted by a surge in battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales ahead of the September 30 expiration of a consumer EV tax credit. Analysts at S&P Global Mobility expect a subsequent "BEV volume hangover," combined with ongoing vehicle affordability issues, to contribute to more moderate growth in the fourth quarter. <7> The Social Security Administration announced a 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2026, which will increase benefits for approximately 75 million Americans. The adjustment will go into effect for benefits payable to nearly 71 million Social Security beneficiaries starting in January 2026, increasing the average retiree's monthly benefit by roughly $56. <8> The annual inflation rate in the United States for the 12 months ending in September 2025 was 3.0%, an increase from the 2.9% rate recorded in August. This rate matches the previous high for the year, which was also 3.0% in January 2025. The monthly increase in the all items index was largely driven by a 4.1% rise in the gasoline index. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, slowed to 3.0% over the 12 months ending in September, down from 3.1% in August. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) data for September 2025 was published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on October 24, 2025. <9> The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased by 0.3% in September 2025 on a seasonally adjusted basis, following a 0.4% rise in August, as announced on October 24, 2025. Over the 12 months prior to September, the all items index saw an increase of 3.0% before seasonal adjustment. The primary contributors to the monthly increase included shelter, airline fares, recreation, household furnishings and operations, and apparel.
